column5: God refuge versus flight to mountain
column6: The commentary's endangered person is offered a mountain as a false refuge; the psalmist says he takes refuge in the LORD and challenges advice to flee like a bird to a mountain.
The commentary's shelter protects a person trapped by calamity; the speaker takes refuge beneath divine wings until the destructive storm has passed.
The commentary joins safety, faith, and family belonging; Boaz says Ruth has left her old household and come to seek refuge under Israel's God's wings.
The commentary's lineage becomes a refuge with a human guarantor beside the endangered; Ruth asks Boaz to spread his garment or wing over her because he is a family redeemer.
The commentary cites asylum for a threatened outsider and safe passage; this appeal asks that outcasts be allowed to stay and sheltered from a destroyer.
The commentary's asylum means protecting someone who has fled danger; the law forbids handing an escaped slave back to his master.
The commentary calls a secure dwelling the destination of asylum; the escaped slave may live among Israel wherever he chooses without oppression.
The commentary's endangered person clings to a supposed shelter; Joab flees from judgment and grasps the altar's horns, testing whether a sacred place can protect him.
The commentary's false refuge cannot avert loss; Joab is struck down after grasping the altar, so physical contact with the sanctuary does not save him.
The commentary contrasts a true exception from ruin with false sanctuary; the law orders a deliberate killer taken even from God's altar for execution.
The commentary describes a threatened person's act of clinging; Adonijah grasps the altar horns after fearing Solomon, a second biblical test of sanctuary as refuge.
The commentary's refuge requires more than a physical grip; Solomon makes Adonijah's safety conditional on worthy conduct after he has seized the altar.
The commentary warns that a shelter can be false; the bramble invites the trees to take refuge in its shade while threatening destructive fire, an image of a dangerous protector.
The commentary locates rescue amid imminent loss; Nahum calls the LORD a stronghold on a day of trouble and says he knows those taking refuge in him.
The commentary pairs refuge with overwhelming destruction; the next verse makes floodlike annihilation the fate of God's adversaries, sharpening the protected group's exception.

column5: divine presence through water and fire
column6: The commentary's safety is accompaniment through apparently inescapable danger; God promises to be with Israel through rivers and fire so neither destroys them.

column5: lowly remnant seeks refuge in name
column6: The commentary reads belief as entry into a safe community; God leaves a humble people who take refuge in the LORD's name.
The commentary joins guarded truth and freedom from fear in the saved group; the remnant neither lies nor acts unjustly and lies down with no one to frighten it.
The commentary emphasizes mutual counsel among those escaping loss; people who fear the LORD speak to one another and their words are heard and recorded by God.
The commentary makes lineage and communal faith a shelter; God promises to spare those recorded as his own as a father spares a serving son.
The commentary's sabir stands beside others as their protection; Isaiah describes a human figure as shelter from wind and storm and shade like a great rock.
The commentary calls the secure city a place of refuge; Zion receives a canopy that shelters people from heat, storm, and rain.
The commentary's son trusts a mountain but needs true protection; God says those taking refuge in him will possess the holy mountain, reversing the mountain's role from savior to gift.
The commentary places faith against destruction with no escape; Daniel's companions declare that the God they serve can rescue them from the king's blazing furnace.
The commentary's sabir remains with the community in its ordeal; the king sees a fourth figure walking alongside the three men within the furnace.

column5: Aramaic אמנ / ء م ن; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary connects trusting faith with survival; after Daniel leaves the lions' den unharmed, the narrative explicitly attributes this to his trust in God using Aramaic אמנ.

column5: חסר / خ س ر; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary opposes human loss to secure reliance on God; even young lions hunger, but seekers of the LORD lack no good thing, using Hebrew חסר for concrete want.

column5: חקק / ح ق ق; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's truth is a duty to protect; Wisdom says rulers decree justice through her, using Hebrew חקק for enacting what is right rather than an exact translation of Arabic حق.

column5: חקק / ح ق ق; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary's guarded truth has a public consequence; Isaiah condemns those who decree unjust decrees, using Hebrew חקק for the dangerous inversion of a protective rule.
The commentary defines the believer's safe place as a home; this verse says the worshipper has made the Most High his dwelling refuge.
The commentary's secure house counters an inescapable disaster; the psalm promises that evil and plague will not approach the worshipper's tent.
The commentary's exception moves believers out of destructive loss; Jesus' saying promises that whoever believes will not perish but have life.
The commentary reads faith as entry into safety; Jesus says a hearer who believes has already passed from death to life and avoids judgment.

The commentary's exception names both faith and good deeds; Paul envisages a builder whose work burns and who suffers loss yet is himself saved through fire, distinguishing the person's rescue from the work's survival.
The commentary gives patience a secondary image of a disaster without an exit; Paul says God provides a way out of trial precisely so the tested person can endure it.
The commentary's sabir is a guarantor who stays with the group; Hebrews explicitly makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.
The commentary's communal guarantor accompanies people into security; Hebrews says Jesus lives to intercede and can save those who approach God through him.
The commentary joins patience to right action and deliverance; Hebrews says the hearers need endurance so that after doing God's will they receive the promise.
The commentary defines belief as protection against loss; Peter describes his addressees as guarded by God's power through faith for a salvation to be revealed.

column5: good deeds amid suffering and trust
column6: The commentary's exception unites faith, righteous action, and patience under danger; Peter tells sufferers to entrust themselves to a faithful Creator while doing good.

column5: stand firm in faith with suffering kin
column6: The commentary's sabir remains beside the group; Peter calls believers to resist the adversary firm in faith, knowing their wider brotherhood shares the same sufferings.
The commentary makes counsel in truth and patience mutual duties; Paul directs Timothy to correct, rebuke, and encourage with complete patience and teaching.

column5: turn back a wanderer from truth
column6: The commentary calls truth something one protects for another; James addresses anyone who restores a person straying from truth.
The commentary's communal guarantor prevents another's ruin; James says bringing back the wanderer saves a soul from death.
The commentary pictures people at the edge of destruction needing communal rescue; Jude commands others to be saved by being snatched from fire.

column5: persist in good deeds until harvest
column6: The commentary's saved group combines good acts with patience; Paul says not to grow weary in doing good because the harvest comes if they do not give up.

column5: kept word of endurance, protected in trial
column6: The commentary connects patience and truth with safety; the speaker promises to keep a community from the coming hour of testing because it kept his word of endurance.

column5: hold fast so crown not taken
column6: The commentary's saving action is to keep a firm hold; the church is told to hold what it has so no one takes its crown.
The commentary links rescue at an edge to a group standing with the endangered; Paul's disciples lower him in a basket through the city wall to escape a plot against his life.
The commentary opposes fear with secure faith; after Jesus stills a dangerous storm, he asks his terrified companions where their faith is.

column5: father receives lost son at home
column6: The commentary makes ancestry and home a place of return from loss; the father runs to embrace the returning son while he is still far off.

column5: lost and dead son found alive
column6: The commentary uses loss for destruction and a familial refuge for escape; the father describes the restored son as formerly dead and lost but now alive and found.

column5: truth to neighbors as shared body
column6: The commentary requires people to guard truth together; Paul commands each to speak truth to a neighbor because believers are members of one another.
The commentary's exception can be pictured as arriving at a saving place; Jesus contrasts a broad gate and road that carry many toward destruction.
The commentary's escaped group must find the right entry; Jesus says the narrow gate and hard road lead to life and few find them.

column5: stranger moves injured man to shelter
column6: The commentary's sabir stays with the endangered and helps him reach safety; the Samaritan binds the wounded stranger, carries him to an inn, and cares for him.
The commentary defines sabir as one who guarantees a community member's welfare; the Samaritan pays the innkeeper and promises to repay further costs.
The commentary's sabir acts as a guarantor beside someone vulnerable; Paul asks Philemon to charge Onesimus's wrong or debt to Paul himself.
The commentary's communal surety takes responsibility for another's exposure; Paul writes his own pledge to repay Onesimus's debt.
The commentary's asylum extends protection to an outsider; the elder praises work done faithfully for traveling brothers who were strangers to the host.
The commentary's quoted asylum includes bringing a protected outsider to a safe destination; the elder asks the host to send the travelers onward in a manner worthy of God.
The commentary's sabir accompanies the endangered to safety; the Mishnah sends two learned escorts with a killer fleeing toward a refuge city so the avenger does not kill him on the way.

The commentary says truth must be protected by mutual correction; this discussion says apparently righteous people in a doomed city were not exempt when they could have protested wrongdoing but did not.
The commentary's sabir stays beside the group as a refuge; Sirach calls a faithful friend a strong shelter discovered by the person who finds one.

column5: strive for truth, God fights for you
column6: The commentary treats truth as a charge one must defend; Sirach commands striving for truth even to death and promises God's defense in return.

column5: עצר / ع ص ر; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary links calamity without an exit to seeking refuge; Solomon describes heaven shut up with no rain and directs the afflicted to pray toward the sanctuary, while Hebrew עצר means restraint rather than the Arabic shelter sense.

column5: חקק / ح ق ق; table sound correspondence
column6: The commentary calls truth something one must preserve; Job wishes his defending words inscribed permanently, using Hebrew חקק for inscription rather than Arabic حق as truth.

column5: mountains as questioned source of help
column6: The commentary quotes a son treating a mountain as protection; the pilgrim looks to the mountains and asks where help comes from, without yet identifying the mountains as rescuers.
The commentary separates a mountain's apparent shelter from divine rescue; the pilgrim answers that help comes from the LORD who made heaven and earth.

column5: watchmen guard city and call God
column6: The commentary joins protected city and communal responsibility; appointed watchmen on Jerusalem's walls give God no silence as they call for the city's restoration.
The commentary's safe city can become an unsafe shelter; Jeremiah tells Benjamin's people to flee out of Jerusalem because disaster is coming from the north.
The commentary's exception links right action with escape from destruction; the prophet tells the humble to seek righteousness and humility so they may be hidden on the day of wrath.
The commentary's refuge averts destruction; the psalmist calls God a hiding place who preserves him from trouble and surrounds him with cries of deliverance.

column5: refuge in God over reliance on people
column6: The commentary warns against a false hold; this proverb-like psalm line says taking refuge in the LORD is better than trusting human beings.
The commentary reads safety as a place people may enter in need; Hebrews invites a confident approach to the throne of grace for mercy and help at the needed time.
The commentary's sabir accompanies and guarantees the endangered; Hebrews presents Jesus as a forerunner who enters the inner sanctuary on the people's behalf.

column5: friends carry helpless man through roof
column6: The commentary's communal protector helps an endangered person reach safety; companions bring a paralyzed man to Jesus by opening a roof and lowering his mat when the crowd blocks access.
The commentary links collective faith to rescue; Jesus sees the faith of those bringing the paralyzed man and addresses the man with forgiveness.
The commentary's no-exit calamity meets endurance; Paul says his group is afflicted and perplexed but neither crushed nor driven to despair.
The commentary places patient company against annihilation; Paul says the group is persecuted and struck down yet neither abandoned nor destroyed.

column5: love enacted in deed and truth
column6: The commentary's exception includes righteous deeds and protected truth; the letter insists that love be practiced in deed and truth rather than only in speech.
The commentary's asylum scene grants protection to an outsider; the king identifies hospitality to a stranger as care rendered to him.
The commentary's quoted safe conduct for an outsider has a communal counterpart; Hebrews commands hospitality to strangers and recalls hosts who unknowingly welcomed angels.
The commentary's sabir supports a group in its affairs; Paul asks the Roman believers to aid Phoebe, who has been a patron and helper of many, including him.

column5: work survives fire and receives reward
column6: The commentary links righteous works to surviving loss; immediately before the saved builder whose work burns, Paul says enduring work earns a reward after fire tests it.

column5: iron prison gate opens for escape
column6: The commentary's no-exit peril yields to rescue; Peter passes the guards and an iron gate opens of itself as he leaves confinement.
The commentary glosses security as fear's opposite; the letter says perfected love casts out fear, connecting safety to a tested communal relation rather than using its word for faith.

column5: refuge residents supplied by priestly mothers
column6: The commentary's guarantor helps a trapped community endure; this Mishnah says mothers of high priests gave food and clothing to exiles in refuge cities so the exiles would not pray for their sons' deaths.
The commentary makes counsel in truth a protective duty; the rabbinic discussion treats rebuking a fellow person as obligatory while debating its limits and how to avoid harm.

column5: Noah's ark read as saving community
column6: The commentary's flood refuge and faithful household meet Augustine's reading of the ark as a figure of Christ and the church, extending the vessel's shelter to a community.
The commentary's flood scene asks where rescue is found; Justin reads Noah's household saved through water as a figure of salvation associated with baptism.

column5: righteous souls held in God's hand
column6: The commentary's secure hold faces apparent annihilation; Wisdom places righteous souls in God's hand beyond torment, making safety persist beyond physical death.
The commentary opposes fear and loss with faith; Sirach asks readers to recall whether anyone who trusted the Lord was ever forsaken.
